variables.romance: no one to toast the thaw with

blocks.text: The house does not so much rise from the hill as refuse to let it go.

blocks.alt: Frostmere Hall at dusk, snow already gathering on its dark roofline.

blocks.text: Frostmere Hall sits at the end of a mile of unlit drive, and the snow that started an hour ago hasn't let up since. You're here on ordinary business — the Star, the sale, a signature on a valuation you could have mailed in — but ordinary business has never once explained why a house this size keeps its lamps lit at every window at half past six.

choices.text: Ring the bell

blocks.text: A young woman opens the door herself before the bell has finished — Helena Frostmere, you'd guess, from the family portraits you were sent ahead of the appraisal. "You made it," she says, glancing past you at the weather like it's a guest she didn't invite. "Another hour and you wouldn't have."
She takes your coat. "My father's looking forward to this. He talks about that sapphire like it's a person."

choices.text: Ask how bad the roads really are
Ask about the family gathered for the evening

blocks.text: "Bad enough that the last car through was two hours ago, and that was the doctor." Helena shrugs off the question the way people do when they've already decided not to worry about it. "We're stocked for a week. We always are, out here."

choices.text: Head on in

blocks.text: "Everyone who matters to the estate, one way or another," Helena says, with a small, dry edge you file away. "My stepmother. My brother, when he bothers. Dr. Vane, who's practically furniture. Mrs. Pruett, who runs the place better than any of us. And Nathaniel — my fiancé, though my father would rather I hadn't said that out loud."

choices.text: Ask to see the Star before you do anything else
Head on in

blocks.text: Helena laughs, briefly, at your professionalism, and takes you to the study herself — Alistair isn't down yet, but the case sits on his desk, and he's left it unlocked for exactly this. Inside, on dark velvet, the Frostmere Star is exactly as striking as the file promised: a sapphire the size of a thumbnail, cut in a way that catches even the grey afternoon light and does something with it.

blocks.alt: A large sapphire on dark velvet, catching pale light through a study window.

blocks.text: It's the reason you're in this house at all. By tomorrow morning, it will be the least interesting thing in it.

choices.text: Head on in to meet everyone properly

blocks.text: The drawing room holds the rest of them, arranged like a hand of cards nobody's decided to play yet. **Cassandra Frostmere**, Alistair's second wife, twenty years his junior and aware of it, offers you a hand and a smile that doesn't reach anywhere past her mouth. **Julian**, the son, is at the sideboard with a glass he's already refilled once. **Dr. Emory Vane** rises to greet you properly, warm in the specific way of a man used to being liked. **Mrs. Agatha Pruett**, the housekeeper, hovers at the door with the air of someone counting heads. And **Nathaniel Reyes** sits a little apart, watching Helena more than he's watching you.
Alistair Frostmere himself is upstairs, Helena says — he'll come down for dinner, and he'll want to show you the Star himself, first, before anyone else gets a word in.

choices.text: Go through to dinner

blocks.text: Alistair Frostmere comes down exactly once, for exactly long enough to be the most interesting person at his own table — sharp, funny, needling everyone by turns, the Star's velvet case sitting unopened by his elbow like a promise he's enjoying making you wait for. "After," he tells you, when you ask. "Let an old man have his dinner first."

Under the performance, the table has its own weather. Julian doesn't meet his father's eye. Cassandra's hand finds Alistair's sleeve once, briefly, and he doesn't notice or pretends not to. Nathaniel says almost nothing, and Alistair addresses almost nothing to him.

choices.text: Watch the room a little longer
Let the evening carry you along

blocks.text: Dr. Vane laughs too readily at things that aren't especially funny — the laugh of a man keeping a room comfortable on purpose. Once, when Alistair mentions "settling accounts before the new year," you catch Vane's smile hold a half-second too long, like a held breath. Mrs. Pruett, refilling glasses, goes very still at the same words, then keeps moving as if she hadn't.

choices.text: Watch a little longer still

blocks.text: Alistair, oblivious or enjoying it, presses on: "Emory here thinks I ought to slow down. I keep telling him I intend to outlive every doctor who's ever told me that." It's meant as a joke. Nobody at the table quite laughs at it the way a joke usually earns.

choices.text: File it away for later

blocks.text: By the time dessert is cleared, the windows have gone from grey to black, and the wind has found a register it likes and stayed there. Mrs. Pruett comes in without knocking to say the telephone line has gone dead, and that the drive is impassable in either direction — has been for an hour, if she's honest.
"Well," Alistair says, into the small silence that follows, with the particular relish of a man who enjoys being the only one unbothered. "Then we're all guests here tonight, aren't we."

choices.text: Head upstairs for the night

blocks.text: Helena shows you to a guest room at the end of the east wing, the Star's case still unopened downstairs — Alistair changed his mind about tonight, sent word he was tired, promised the morning instead. The house settles into the particular quiet of somewhere old and full of wind.

choices.text: Take a short walk through the halls before bed
Go straight to sleep

blocks.text: The corridor lamps are turned low. Passing Alistair's study, you notice light still under the door and the murmur of two voices — one his, one you don't place before a floorboard gives you away and the murmur stops. By the time you're past, the door hasn't opened.
Whoever it was, they didn't want to be seen leaving.

choices.text: Go on to bed

blocks.text: Sleep comes slower than the hour deserves. The wind has a way of sounding, in an old house, like someone testing every door in turn.

choices.text: Morning

blocks.text: A scream — thin, cut short, Mrs. Pruett's — pulls you out of bed before you've finished waking. It's coming from the study.

choices.text: Go

blocks.text: Alistair Frostmere is at his own desk, head down over the blotter as if he'd simply fallen asleep working — except for the stillness, and the smell of bitter almonds that isn't quite right for anything natural, and the fact that the study door was locked from the inside and Mrs. Pruett had to use her master key to get in at all.

blocks.alt: A locked study at dawn, snow-grey light through tall windows, a figure slumped at the desk.

blocks.text: He's cold. He has been for hours.

choices.text: Take in the room before anyone else disturbs it

blocks.text: The window is latched from inside. The fireplace still holds a little warmth and a little ash that isn't all wood. A leather appointment book lies open on the desk, and beside Alistair's hand, half-hidden under a stack of correspondence, the Star's velvet case sits closed — untouched, as far as you can tell without opening it.
Whatever happened here, it wasn't a robbery. Not directly.

choices.text: One more look before you call the others

blocks.text: A small brass key sits in the top drawer, unremarkable except that it matches nothing in the room — not the desk, not the cabinet, not the window latch. A key kept for a lock that isn't in this study at all.

choices.text: Let the household in

blocks.text: The house comes apart in the ordinary ways a house does around a death — Cassandra goes white and silent, Julian goes loud and then ashamed of being loud, Helena holds herself together by holding Mrs. Pruett together first. Nathaniel says almost nothing, which you're starting to recognize as the thing he does instead of showing anything at all. Dr. Vane, professionally, is the first to kneel by the body — checks for a pulse that was never going to be there, and pronounces him gone with a steadiness that could be training or could be something else.

choices.text: Ask about reaching the police

blocks.text: The line is still dead. The drive is still buried. Whatever happened in this house last night, the house is going to have to sit with it — everyone in it, together, for at least a day, maybe two — before anyone from outside can reach them at all.
You realize, with the specific discomfort of being handed something you didn't ask for, that you're the only person under this roof who's ever had to think about a crime scene professionally.

choices.text: Decide what to do about that

blocks.text: Helena finds you first, in the hall outside the study, and doesn't waste time getting to it. "You do this," she says — not quite a question. "Insurance work, provenance, all of it — you have to know how to look at things properly. I need you to look at this properly. Before it's six people in a locked house lying to each other for a week and calling it grief."

choices.text: Agree to look into it

blocks.text: You start where every investigation starts — with the room, and the people, and the long list of things everyone is choosing not to say yet. Somewhere under this roof is a killer who is, right now, having breakfast with the rest of the household as though nothing has changed at all.

choices.text: Begin

blocks.text: The house is trapped, and so is everyone in it — which means, for as long as the snow holds, this room and the people in it *are* the case. There's a great deal still to look at, and no one is going anywhere.

You've learned enough here — move on

blocks.text: The burned letter's one surviving line isn't the only scrap in that grate, once you go back with better light and more patience — three more fragments, smaller, blacker, barely holding together.

choices.text: Try to piece the fragments in the order they'd have been written
Try to piece them in the order they'd have burned — last page first

blocks.text: Read forward, the fragments refuse to agree with each other — half-sentences that don't connect, a false start you've mistaken for a middle. You've singed your patience along with the paper.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Burned pages curl from the last line first — read backward through the burning, the fragments finally agree with each other: **"...board. I am not the only one who remembers what happened. If you go through with this, you will not be the only one who suffers for it."**

Someone was threatening more than Vane's reputation. Someone told him he wasn't the only one who'd pay if the truth came out — which means whatever Alistair knew, it wasn't only about one bad year with one patient.

onEnter.value: the rest of the burned letter, read backward through the ash

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Mrs. Pruett, of everyone in the house, is the one who actually knows the family's longer history — the grandfather who built the fortune on shipping, the uncle who nearly lost it in a bad decade, Alistair's own long, slow rise into a man who never once, in her memory, apologized for anything.

choices.text: Ask if he'd made enemies like that before

blocks.text: "He made them the way some men make friends," she says, "without especially trying, and without especially minding once he had. Most of them stayed enemies at a comfortable distance. I couldn't tell you, hand on heart, which ones might have stopped keeping that distance."

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Alistair's business affairs turn out to be exactly as dull as business affairs usually are — shipping contracts, a dispute over a warehouse lease, nothing that reads like a motive for murder, however hard you squint at it. It's the one part of this man's life, it seems, that stayed entirely ordinary right up until it ended.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: The Star's paperwork is, professionally, the most straightforward thing in this entire house — a clean chain of ownership back three generations, nothing forged, nothing missing, no reason at all for anyone to have wanted Alistair dead over a jewel with a file this tidy.
It's almost a relief, working through something in this house that turns out to be exactly what it claims to be.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Cassandra has claimed the conservatory as her own since the wedding, the way a person claims one room in a house that was never quite theirs. Orchids that must have cost more than most people's rent line the glass; she waters them with a kind of stubborn attention that has nothing to do with grief.

choices.text: Ask her why this room

blocks.text: "It's the one room in this house he never much cared for," she says, not looking up from the watering can. "Too much upkeep for too little to show. I liked that about it. I liked having something that was only mine."
It isn't an alibi and it isn't a confession. It's just a woman who married into a house that was never built to hold her comfortably, telling you so, in her own way.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: The attic holds three generations of Frostmere paperwork, most of it dull, some of it not — old ledgers, older photographs, a christening record for Helena with a date that, held up against the family's own telling of things, doesn't quite add up the way everyone's always let it.

blocks.alt: A dusty attic, trunks and old photographs, pale light through a single small window.

choices.text: Put it back and say nothing yet

blocks.text: You already have the shape of what this means from Mrs. Pruett, and the paper only confirms it. It's not evidence of a murder. It's evidence of a much older, much quieter kind of keeping — a family holding its own history at arm's length for a very long time.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: The storm itself is the one witness in this house that hasn't lied to anyone yet — the gate that banged at half nine, the tea at a quarter past, the wind that would have covered footsteps but not swallowed them entirely. Testing each account against it, one at a time, seems worth the hours.

Check Julian's account
Check Mrs. Pruett's account

Check Dr. Vane's account
You've tested enough of them

blocks.text: Cassandra's account — her room, alone, from half nine — holds up against the one person who'd know: Helena, who remembers passing her stepmother's door and hearing her moving about inside, right around the time the gate went.

choices.text: Cross her off, at least for the murder itself

blocks.text: Whatever else Cassandra Frostmere is carrying, the timeline itself has nothing to say against her.

choices.text: Back to the timeline

blocks.text: Julian's account holds too, if less comfortably — a maid confirms hearing him through his door, restless and drinking, well past midnight, in a room he clearly never left.

choices.text: Cross him off too

blocks.text: A man too drunk to stand steadily is, at least, a man with a fairly convincing reason not to have committed a careful, quiet murder that same night.

choices.text: Back to the timeline

blocks.text: Mrs. Pruett's own account is the one you already trust most, if only because she's the one who gave you the timeline to test everyone else against in the first place. It holds up against her own staff's memory of her, moving through the house on her usual rounds.

choices.text: Note that, and move on

blocks.text: If she'd wanted to lie about her own movements that night, she'd have had every opportunity to build herself a better alibi than the one the rest of the staff can independently confirm.

choices.text: Back to the timeline

blocks.text: Nathaniel's account is thin — alone in his room, he says, with nothing and no one to confirm it — but thin isn't the same as false, and nothing about the storm's own timeline puts him anywhere near the study specifically.

choices.text: Leave it as unresolved, for now

blocks.text: An unconfirmed alibi is a mark against a man, but it isn't the same thing as evidence he was somewhere in particular. You'll need more than his silence to build a case around him.

choices.text: Back to the timeline

blocks.text: Dr. Vane's account is the one that doesn't survive contact with the timeline at all — his claimed nine o'clock bedtime sits squarely inside the window between Mrs. Pruett's tea and the gate banging shut, and no one in this house can place him anywhere but exactly where the study was.

choices.text: Lay the whole cross-check out plainly

blocks.text: Five accounts tested against the one witness that can't be flattered or frightened into lying — the storm itself — and only one of them fails to hold. That's not proof by itself. It's a very hard thing to explain away.

onEnter.value: a full cross-check: every account holds up but his

choices.text: Back to the timeline

blocks.text: Room by room, most of the guest wing gives up nothing more than the ordinary disorder of people who packed for a weekend and got a siege instead. Cassandra's room is tidier than grief usually allows for. Julian's smells of last night's whisky.

choices.text: Look more carefully at Nathaniel's room

blocks.text: Nathaniel's room is the only one in the wing with a lamp burned down past where an early bedtime would explain, and a wastebasket with several false starts of handwriting screwed up and thrown away — practice, you realize, at forging a hand that isn't his own.
It fits what the safe already told you. It doesn't tell you anything the safe hadn't already.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: The gatehouse sits empty most of the year — a groundskeeper's cottage nobody's used since the last one retired — but the snow around its door shows one set of footprints, days old now, half-filled in, leading up to it and not away again.

blocks.alt: A small stone gatehouse at the edge of the estate, half-buried in snow, a single blurred trail of footprints leading to its door.

choices.text: Go in and have a look

blocks.text: Inside, dust and cold and nothing recent — except a spare set of keys on a board by the door, one hook empty where the study's spare should hang. It's been gone long enough that the dust around the other hooks has settled evenly around the gap.
Someone took that key before the storm ever started. This wasn't decided the night Alistair died. It was decided before.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Aldous Whitfield, the Frostmere family's solicitor for longer than Helena's been alive, was here on business of his own the night of the storm and has been quietly, correctly horrified by everything since. "I came up to update a beneficiary line on a policy," he says. "A small thing. I did not come up for this."

choices.text: Ask him about the will

blocks.text: "There is exactly one valid will," Whitfield says, precise as a man who's spent a career being precise, "and it sits in my office safe, not this house's. Anything found here claiming otherwise is, at best, a draft. At worst—" He stops himself, professionally, before finishing that sentence for you.
Whatever the codicil in Alistair's own safe was meant to accomplish, Whitfield's testimony is enough, on its own, to make sure it never would have.

choices.text: Ask if Alistair had any recent disputes worth knowing about

blocks.text: Whitfield hesitates in a way lawyers hesitate when the honest answer and the discreet answer aren't the same thing, then decides, visibly, that a dead client's discretion has run its course.

choices.text: Wait him out

blocks.text: "Alistair filed a formal complaint against Emory Vane with the medical board, six weeks ago. A patient Vane lost, some years back, that Alistair had only recently learned the full circumstances of. He was going to see it through — he told me himself he intended to, whatever it cost their friendship."
A friendship built on thirty years doesn't survive a complaint like that easily. A man's whole career might not survive it at all.

onEnter.value: Whitfield's account of Alistair's complaint to the medical board

choices.text: Ask what he was doing here so late in the year

blocks.text: "The policy," Whitfield says again, a little apologetically, as if it embarrasses him now to have come all this way for something so ordinary. "Alistair asked me to update it just last week. Nothing unusual in the change itself. Unusual, perhaps, in the timing, now that I think of it properly."

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: You find Helena going through her father's correspondence with the particular grim focus of someone who needs a task more than she needs comfort. She talks, unprompted, about the father he was before all this — sharper stories than the grief-softened ones people usually offer.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Ines has taken over a corner of the library as an unofficial press room, notes pinned up in a shorthand only she can read. "You want to know what I think," she says, not quite a question, and tells you anyway — a theory about Vane that's closer to right than she has any evidence yet to justify.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: A full formal dinner, everyone present, feels almost obscene given the circumstances — and yet the household keeps having them, out of habit or denial or simple hunger, and there's more to learn watching six people perform normalcy around a table than in half your interviews.

choices.text: Watch who avoids whose eye

blocks.text: Cassandra and Julian have found an easy, wary alliance since the death, the way people sometimes do when they've decided the same person isn't the threat. Nathaniel watches Helena more than his plate. Mrs. Pruett serves everyone with the exact same careful attention she always has, including the one person at that table she has more reason than most to watch closely.

Dr. Vane, throughout, remains the most relaxed person in the room. Either that means something, or it means he's simply better at this than everyone else here — and you're not yet sure those are different things.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: In daylight the study gives up more than it did at dawn. The window latch is intact and painted shut besides — no one came or went that way. The door lock is a good one, the kind that takes a proper key, not a hairpin.

choices.text: Work out how the killer left a locked room

blocks.text: Three ways a locked room stops being locked: the door was never really locked from a witness's honest memory, someone used a second way in nobody's thought of, or someone had a key that wasn't supposed to exist.
The window's painted shut and the paint isn't disturbed. That rules out the obvious way out — which leaves two real theories worth testing.

choices.text: Theory: a secret passage behind the bookshelf
Theory: someone besides Alistair had a key

blocks.text: You spend a good hour tapping panelling that turns out to be exactly as solid as it looks. Frostmere Hall, disappointingly, is not that kind of house. You've lost time you didn't have to lose.

choices.text: Back to the study door

blocks.text: The lock is old but not unique — the kind a household would keep a spare key for, in case a study door ever needed opening without waking the man inside it. Someone with reason to be trusted with that spare could have let themselves in, done what they came to do, and locked it again behind them on the way out.
Which means you're not looking for someone who broke in. You're looking for someone the house already trusted with a key.

choices.text: Look over the rest of the room

blocks.text: In the cold grate, mostly ash, one scrap of a burned letter has survived enough to read: **"...cannot let you ruin what's left of my name over an old mistake. I will not be threatened in my own—"** and there it stops, curling black at the edge.
Someone was blackmailing Alistair Frostmere. Or Alistair was refusing to be blackmailed — which, going by what happened to him, may amount to the same thing.

onEnter.value: a burned letter, half a threat

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: The library still smells of the pipe Alistair wasn't supposed to smoke in it. His appointment book sits where Mrs. Pruett left it for you, open to last night's page.

choices.text: Try to make sense of the appointment book

blocks.text: Most of the page is ordinary — meals, a call about the estate, Helena's name twice underlined. But the last entry for the evening isn't in plain hand at all:
E.V. — IX — HW GRWWOH LW
A concordance sits in the same drawer, in Alistair's writing — a simple shift, the kind a man invents for himself and no one else. Line the cipher up against it.

choices.text: Read it as a shift of one letter back
Read it as a shift of one letter forward

blocks.text: Shifted the wrong way, the message dissolves into nonsense. You've burned a candle's worth of time on it and have nothing to show for the effort.

choices.text: Move on to the will

blocks.text: Shifted forward, it resolves clean: **F.W. — IX — WE SETTLE IT.**

F.W. isn't a name in this house. But E.V. — read correctly as the two initials that matter, the ones that make sense of everyone else's evening — is Emory Vane. Alistair summoned his own physician to the study at nine o'clock last night, to settle something.

onEnter.value: the coded appointment: Vane, nine o'clock

choices.text: Move on to the will

blocks.text: A study wall safe is common enough in a house this old, and Alistair's is hidden, not very well, behind the portrait of his own father — the kind of hiding place a man chooses so he can find it easily himself. It wants a combination he never wrote down.
He was a man of habits, though, and habits are their own kind of writing, if you know where to read them.

choices.text: Try the year Frostmere & Co. was founded
Try the date on his father's portrait

blocks.text: The dial clicks past the wrong number three times running. You give it up before you jam the mechanism entirely.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: The portrait's brass plate carries a date Alistair mentioned twice at dinner without meaning to teach anyone anything — and the safe opens on the third try. Inside: cash, a jewel case that isn't the Star's, and a second will, dated three months after the one his solicitor holds, naming an amended set of beneficiaries in a hand that is almost, but not quite, Alistair's own.
Someone forged a codicil to this will. Whoever it favors most is the person with the most reason to have wanted it believed real.

onEnter.value: a forged codicil to the will

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Dr. Vane keeps a small private study off the surgery he uses for the household — mostly harmless things, tinctures and dressings, but a locked case holds what a country doctor actually needs for the bad nights.

blocks.alt: A physician's study: glass-fronted cabinets, small labelled bottles, a worn leather case.

blocks.text: One bottle in the case is nearly empty, and wiped clean of dust in a way none of its neighbors are.

choices.text: Work out what it held

blocks.text: The label's gone, but the case notes in Vane's own hand describe the symptoms of three things he keeps on hand for entirely legitimate reasons — and only one of them, in the wrong dose, stops a heart quietly enough to look, to an untrained eye, like sleep.

choices.text: Guess arsenic
Guess digitalis — foxglove, in the wrong hands

blocks.text: Arsenic leaves its own signs, and Alistair had none of them. You've spent time chasing the wrong poison, and the bottle sits there, still unexplained.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Digitalis — a heart medicine in the correct dose, a quiet killer in the wrong one, and exactly the kind of thing a physician would have on hand without anyone thinking twice about the bottle going missing. The vial in the study bookshelf, you realize, is the twin of the empty one here — the same maker's glass.

onEnter.value: a matched pair of digitalis vials

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Cassandra receives you in the morning room with the particular composure of someone who has rehearsed being asked this. "I loved him," she says, before you've asked anything at all. "Whatever else you hear in this house, start there."
Asked where she was after eleven, she says her room, alone, and doesn't offer it as if she expects to be believed.

choices.text: Ask what "whatever else you hear" means

blocks.text: She goes very still, then decides, visibly, to get ahead of it. "There's a man — was, is, I don't know anymore — who isn't my husband. It ended months ago and it has nothing to do with any of this, except that it will look like everything to you, so I'd rather you heard it from me than from Mrs. Pruett's face when the subject comes up."

A love affair is a motive for a great many things. Murder isn't usually first among them, but you file the letters she describes — still in her writing desk, she admits, foolishly kept — as worth finding.

onEnter.value: Cassandra's love letters, kept when they shouldn't have been

choices.text: Ask if Alistair knew

blocks.text: "He knew," she says, flat. "He'd known for months. He never said a word about it to me directly — just started talking, more and more, about the prenuptial agreement, and how long exactly I had left before it lapsed. That was his way. He punished you by making you wait to find out how."

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Julian is nursing a headache and a second drink he clearly thinks is his first of the day. "Ask it," he says. "Whether I hated him. Everyone else is thinking it."

choices.text: Ask it

blocks.text: "He cut me out of the will two years ago over a debt he decided said something about my character. We hadn't spoken properly since." Julian's hand isn't quite steady around the glass. "I came back for Christmas because Helena begged me to. I didn't come back to fix anything with him. I didn't get the chance, as it turns out."

A bookmaker's letter falls out of his jacket when he shifts — the kind of number that explains a great deal about how badly a man might have wanted his father's money before his father changed his mind about giving it to him.

onEnter.value: a bookmaker's letter in Julian's hand

choices.text: Ask how deep the debt actually runs

blocks.text: He tells you a number he clearly hasn't said out loud to anyone else in this house, and looks almost relieved to have it out of him. "I wasn't going to hurt him over it," he says. "I was going to ask, one more time, and take the no, the way I always do. That's the whole shameful truth of me."

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Dr. Vane is, as ever, easy company — sits you down properly, offers you tea Mrs. Pruett hasn't got round to yet, talks about Alistair with the specific warmth of thirty years' friendship. I told him it was over so I could stay and see this — this marriage, whatever's left of it — through properly. Believe that or don't. It's the truth either way."
Whatever else Cassandra Frostmere is, nothing she's said points to poison, or a locked door, or a study at nine o'clock. An affair explains a marriage. It doesn't, on its own, explain a murder.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Julian, sober for once, is almost relieved to have the debt out in the open. "I owe a bookmaker more than I'd like to say, and I was going to ask my father for it, and he was going to say no, the way he always did. That's the whole of it. I didn't kill him for saying no one more time. I've had a lifetime of practice hearing it."

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Faced with the forged codicil, Nathaniel's careful stillness finally breaks. "I forged it," he says, quiet and fast, like getting it out before he loses his nerve. "Alistair was going to cut Helena off the moment she married me. I thought — if there were already a later will, a fairer one, in his own hand as far as anyone could tell — it would just quietly become true before he could stop it. I never touched him. I didn't have to. I was going to let a piece of paper do it for me."
It's a real crime, and a genuinely damning one, and it isn't murder. A man desperate enough to forge a will is not automatically a man capable of poisoning the person who'd have caught him at it.

choices.text: Back to the household

blocks.text: Mrs. Pruett finally says it outright, in the flat voice of someone who's carried a thing a very long time and is tired of the weight of it. "Helena isn't Cassandra's, and everyone assumes she is, because it's easier than the truth — Alistair's, by a woman who died before she was two, and I raised her the first years myself, and he paid me, all this time, to let the story stay simple."

It's not nothing, as secrets go. It's also, plainly, not a reason to kill Alistair Frostmere — Mrs. Pruett has spent twenty-six years protecting exactly the arrangement his death now threatens to unravel.

blocks.text: You ask Mrs. Pruett to gather the household one last time. She doesn't ask why. She's known, you think, since somewhere around the second day, exactly what this week was always going to end in.

blocks.text: They file into the drawing room the way people file into rooms they've come to dread — Cassandra first, composed as ever; Julian a step behind her, sober tonight in a way that suits him; Nathaniel close to Helena, whatever's left of his standing in this house riding on what happens next; Mrs. Pruett at the door, out of habit, though there's no one left to serve. Dr. Vane comes last, unhurried, and takes the same chair he always takes.

choices.text: Begin

blocks.text: You find Vane alone in his study, and close the door behind you before he can object to that. "You summoned him at nine," you say. "The cipher in his own hand says so. Your alibi doesn't survive Mrs. Pruett's tea, or the gate, or your own missing vial. I don't need you to admit it. I already know."

choices.text: Watch him decide what to do with that

blocks.text: For a long moment he says nothing at all — and then, all at once, thirty years of careful composure simply gives out. "He was going to end me," Vane says, and his voice has none of the warmth left in it now, only something tired and old and finally honest. "Not the practice. Me. One bad year, one patient I couldn't save the way I should have, and he decided to hold it over me forever rather than let it go, the way a friend should have. I told him I wouldn't be threatened. I meant it more than I knew I did."
It isn't a confession made for anyone but himself. It's a confession all the same.

choices.text: Give him a moment before you ask anything more

blocks.text: Neither of you says anything for a while. There isn't, really, anything left that needs saying yet — just the fact of it, sitting in the room with the two of you, until one of you is ready to move again.

choices.text: Ask him what he means to do now

blocks.text: "What I should have done the night I did it, if I'd had any decency left," he says. "Walk down those stairs myself, in the morning, and tell them plainly. I find I'd rather you walked with me than not."

Mrs. Pruett doesn't move at all, and doesn't look surprised, and you understand, watching her, that some part of her worked this out a long time before you said it out loud.
Vane himself says nothing in his own defense — not a denial, not an alibi restated, nothing. In a room built on thirty years of easy warmth, that silence is its own kind of answer.

blocks.text: Dr. Emory Vane is arrested the morning the road finally opens, and goes without the performance of surprise — some part of him, you think, has been waiting to be caught since the moment the cipher went into that appointment book. Frostmere Hall empties out slowly after that, the way houses do once the reason everyone was trapped in them is finally, properly over.

You drive away from Frostmere Hall alone, which is exactly how you arrived, and tell yourself that's not worth minding.

The room you leave Vane standing in isn't convinced enough to hold him, and the county police, when they finally arrive, aren't convinced enough either — a suggestive case, everyone agrees, not a provable one. He stays in the house he's always lived near, practicing medicine, greeting old patients by name, and you never do learn whether the doubt that saved him was reasonable or simply useful.
You leave with everything you actually know and none of the satisfaction of having proven it.

You never do stand up in that drawing room and say his name out loud. What you have instead is quieter and, in its own way, more certain — Emory Vane, alone with you in his own study, telling you the truth because there was, finally, nowhere left in himself to keep it.
He turns himself in the morning the road opens, on his own two feet, before anyone can make him. It isn't justice exactly as the law would build it. It's close enough to hold.

ending.title: What He Told You, Not the Room

blocks.text: Mrs. Agatha Pruett does not come down for breakfast, and by the time anyone thinks to check on her, it's far too late for checking to matter. She had put together, on her own, in her own quiet and careful way, more of the truth than you'd realized — enough to go to Emory Vane alone, thirty years of trust standing between her and any fear she should have had of him.

Whatever you find out after this, about him, about the study, about the cipher and the vial and the gate — it comes too late for the one person in this house who might have deserved to hear it from someone who cared about her.

You say {accused}'s name in front of the whole room, and watch it land the way an accusation lands when it's wrong — not with denial, exactly, but with a kind of bewildered grief that no guilty person has ever quite managed to fake. The county police, when they finally reach the house, find nothing to hold {accused} on, and everything, still, to wonder about everyone else.
Somewhere in this house, Emory Vane spends that same evening being grateful, in private, that you looked everywhere but at him.

ending.title: The Wrong Name in the Room

blocks.text: You don't remember deciding to stop being careful. You remember the cellar stair, and the smell that wasn't right, and then very little else at all — and Frostmere Hall keeps its secret a while longer, the way it's kept every other secret this century, behind good manners and a locked door and a household that has had a great deal of practice not asking questions out loud.

ending.title: One More Thing the House Kept

blocks.text: The murder, in the end, goes unresolved — the county police call it inconclusive, the family calls it closed, and you know it's neither, not really, just a thing everyone involved has decided to stop looking at. What's certain, and provable, and entirely your own fault, is that the Frostmere Star is gone — taken sometime in the days you spent chasing a killer instead of doing the job you actually came to this house to do.
Your firm will have questions. You don't have especially good answers for any of them.

ending.title: The One Thing You Were Actually Hired For

blocks.text: The road opens on a grey morning, and you leave Frostmere Hall with the Star secure in your own case and a killer still sitting somewhere inside it, unnamed, unaccused, free to go on being whoever they've always pretended to be. It isn't failure, exactly. It's just an answer you didn't manage to reach in time.
You'll think about this house, on and off, for a long time after. You never do find out if anyone else ever worked out what you couldn't quite prove.
